heartworm.name: Heartworm
heartworm.summary: Spread by mosquitoes. Worms mature in the heart and lungs and damage them slowly, usually long before any signs show.
heartworm.signs: Persistent cough, tiring quickly on walks, reduced appetite and weight loss. Early infection often has no signs at all.
heartworm.prevention: Preventatives given on a regular schedule wherever mosquitoes are active, with a blood test usually needed before starting. Your vet will advise on testing and timing.

paralysis_tick.name: Paralysis tick
paralysis_tick.summary: A tick of humid coastal Australia whose saliva carries a toxin causing progressive paralysis. It can be fatal without treatment.
paralysis_tick.signs: Wobbly or weak back legs, a changed bark or meow, retching, and laboured breathing. Signs can escalate over hours.
paralysis_tick.prevention: Searching the coat and skin daily, together with a preventative that covers this species. Finding a tick or seeing these signs is an emergency, so contact a vet immediately.

brown_dog_tick.name: Brown dog tick
brown_dog_tick.summary: The one tick that thrives indoors and in kennels, so infestations build up in the home as well as outdoors.
brown_dog_tick.signs: Ticks on the ears, between the toes and around the neck. Heavy burdens can cause anaemia, and this tick also spreads other diseases.
brown_dog_tick.prevention: Treating the pet and the home together, because eggs and juveniles shelter in cracks and bedding. Your vet can advise on both.

blacklegged_tick.name: Deer tick
blacklegged_tick.summary: The main carrier of Lyme disease in North America. It is small, and the nymphs are roughly the size of a poppy seed.
blacklegged_tick.signs: Often nothing from the bite itself. Lyme disease may bring shifting lameness, fever, swollen joints and lethargy weeks later.
blacklegged_tick.prevention: Tick preventatives, checking the coat after time in long grass or woodland, and prompt removal. A Lyme vaccine exists in some regions, so ask your vet.

lone_star_tick.name: Lone star tick
lone_star_tick.summary: An aggressive biter of the southern and eastern United States, recognised by the single pale spot on the female.
lone_star_tick.signs: Visible ticks and irritation at the bite. It can transmit ehrlichiosis, which causes fever, lethargy and bleeding problems.
lone_star_tick.prevention: Tick preventatives and coat checks after time outdoors, particularly along wooded and scrubby edges.

american_dog_tick.name: American dog tick
american_dog_tick.summary: A widespread tick of grassy and open country, and the main carrier of Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
american_dog_tick.signs: Visible ticks, usually around the head and neck. Tick-borne fevers bring lethargy, poor appetite and joint pain.
american_dog_tick.prevention: Tick preventatives, and checking the coat after walks through long grass.

castor_bean_tick.name: Castor bean tick
castor_bean_tick.summary: Europe's most common tick, found in woodland, parks and gardens. It carries Lyme disease and tick-borne encephalitis.
castor_bean_tick.signs: Often nothing at the time. Later signs of tick-borne illness include fever, lameness and lethargy.
castor_bean_tick.prevention: Preventatives through the active season, coat checks after walks, and prompt, complete removal of any tick found.

ornate_dog_tick.name: Ornate dog tick
ornate_dog_tick.summary: A European tick with marbled markings, active earlier and later in the year than most. It transmits babesiosis, which destroys red blood cells.
ornate_dog_tick.signs: Pale gums, dark urine, fever and marked lethargy point to babesiosis and need urgent attention.
ornate_dog_tick.prevention: Preventatives that cover the spring and autumn peaks, plus coat checks after walks in meadow and scrub.

flea.name: Fleas
flea.summary: A year-round problem, because most of the population lives in the home as eggs and larvae rather than on the pet.
flea.signs: Scratching, biting at the base of the tail, flea dirt in the coat, and hair loss. Some pets react severely to a single bite.
flea.prevention: Treating every pet in the household at the same time, alongside washing bedding and vacuuming thoroughly, since the home is the reservoir.

sandfly_leishmania.name: Sandflies
sandfly_leishmania.summary: Small biting flies of the Mediterranean that transmit leishmaniasis, a serious and often lifelong disease.
sandfly_leishmania.signs: Skin sores around the head, hair loss, weight loss, overgrown claws and nosebleeds. Signs can appear months or years after the bite.
sandfly_leishmania.prevention: Repellent products, keeping pets indoors from dusk to dawn, and fine mesh screens. A vaccine is available in some countries, so ask your vet.

lungworm.name: Lungworm
lungworm.summary: Picked up by eating slugs and snails, or grass and toys they have crossed. The worms mature in the heart and lungs.
lungworm.signs: Coughing, tiring easily, and unusual bleeding or bruising that does not stop. This can be life-threatening.
lungworm.prevention: A worming product that specifically covers lungworm, since not all of them do, plus bringing toys and bowls in overnight.

intestinal_worms.name: Intestinal worms
intestinal_worms.summary: Roundworms, hookworms and whipworms, picked up from contaminated soil, faeces or prey. Some can pass to people.
intestinal_worms.signs: Diarrhoea, a pot-bellied look in puppies and kittens, a poor coat, weight loss, and sometimes visible worms in faeces.
intestinal_worms.prevention: Routine worming at a frequency matched to the pet's lifestyle, plus prompt cleanup of faeces. Your vet will advise on how often.
